claim: The baboon gut microbiota was dominated by the phyla Firmicutes (42.2% ± 8.4%), Proteobacteria (13.0% ± 2.8%), Actinobacteria (9.4% ± 4.6%), and Bacteroidetes (7.3% ± 2.4%).

claim: Social interactions directly affect the composition of the gut microbiome in wild baboons.

claim: The results implicate direct, affiliative physical contact as a determinant of gut microbiome composition in natural populations.
source: Unlike prior studies, we were able to exclude kinship, shared diet, and shared environment as the basis for our observations. Our results are thus unique among studies to date in the degree to which they implicate direct, affiliative physical contact as a determinant of gut microbiome composition in natural populations.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on their ability to control for confounding factors.

claim: Social interactions may play a role in the health-related consequences of variation in gut microbiome composition.

claim: The analysis focused on the 327 most prevalent taxa (i.e., those found in at least 50% of hosts).
source: To identify differentially abundant bacterial taxa by social group membership, we used the linear mixed model approach implemented in the program GEMMA (Zhou and Stephens, 2012), which allowed us to account for potential kinship effects in our data set. This approach assumes that the response variable (taxon abundance) is continuously distributed. To meet this assumption, we used methods established for analyzing high-throughput functional genomic data sets (Rapaport et al., 2013). Specifically, we first quantile normalized abundance values across individuals, focusing only on the 327 most prevalent taxa (i.e., those found in at least 50% of hosts based on our MetaPhlAn 2.0 analysis, regardless of abundance), and then transformed the distribution of values for each species to a standard normal.
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical approach and filtering criteria.
